Report_ID: Subjective self-reported frequency of everyday memory problems
Title: Evaluation of NeuroPage as a memory aid for people with multiple sclerosis: A randomised controlled trial
Author: Rachel A Goodwin, Nadina B Lincoln, Roshan das Nair & Andrew Bateman
Comment: Crossover analysis used a paired t-test. The condition-specific available-data counts (27 and 29) are not independent parallel-arm sample sizes and differ from the complete-pair analysis underlying t(24); therefore no independent-groups Hedges g, mean-difference SE, or total analyzed N was computed. Higher EMQ scores indicate worse memory, so synthesis direction would require reversal. The abstract reports p = 0.41 for EMQ, but the detailed Results Table 4 reports p = 0.90; the Table 4 value was extracted. Also, assessment occurred at the end of each two-month condition rather than at a separate 1–6-month post-treatment follow-up.; excluded by outcome classification: does not match the requested outcome/timepoint (meta_analysis_candidate=False); N-DF MISMATCH: n_control(27) + n_treatment(29) − 2 = 54 but reported df=24 — check which N is correct
Design Type: Multicentre, single-blind, randomized controlled crossover trial
Publication Status: Published journal article; published online 20 Mar 2018
Study Environment: Community/home-based intervention; recruited from five UK NHS Trusts and an MS charity event
Medium: SMS text messages delivered to participants’ mobile phones or a pager
Topic of Content: Individualized reminders for personally identified target behaviours versus non-memory/social messages such as news headlines or sports updates
interaction_type: Externally programmed messages transmitted at pre-arranged times
Participant type: Community-dwelling people diagnosed with multiple sclerosis who had self-reported memory problems
Recruitment source: Five UK NHS Trusts and an MS charity event
Outcome measurement: Everyday Memory Questionnaire, 28-item self-report version; scores range from 0 to 112, with higher scores suggesting more frequent forgetting
Outcome variable: Subjective self-reported frequency of everyday memory problems
effect_direction: Lower EMQ scores indicate better subjective memory; the reported near-zero effect indicates essentially no between-condition difference.

Title: Evaluating the efectiveness of cognitive rehabilitation on everyday memory in multiple sclerosis patients
Author: Shokoufeh Mousavi, Hossein Zare & Masoud Etemadifar
Comment: The reported F(2,56)=1.43 is an omnibus comparison across all three groups, not a direct experimental-versus-placebo test. The no-intervention control arm is recorded in additional_group_ns because the schema provides numeric fields for only two groups. No follow-up pairwise comparisons, adjusted group means, or combined-control statistics were reported. M_diff and standardized effects were therefore not calculated. Higher questionnaire scores indicate greater impairment, so effect-direction harmonization would require reverse-coding in synthesis.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: group_1_label ('Experimental group: cognitive/memory rehabilitation') read as the intervention arm, group_2_label ('Placebo group: body relaxation techniques') read as the control arm -- reversed relative to this pipeline's group_1=control/group_2=treatment convention; N-INCONSISTENCY (multi-group): sum of additional_group_ns = 141 ≠ n_total(60) — verify all group Ns
Design Type: Single-blind three-arm randomized controlled trial with repeated assessments
Topic of Content: Compensatory memory strategies, internal and external memory aids, mnemonics, mental review, error-free learning, and individualized adaptation methods
Participant type: People with multiple sclerosis and cognitive impairment
Recruitment source: Patients referred to Isfahan’s multiple sclerosis centre
Outcome measurement: 35-item Everyday Memory Questionnaire; total score ranges from 0 to 175, with higher scores reflecting greater impairment
additional_group_ns: Control group: no rehabilitation intervention, n=20; follow-up mean=120.70, SD=1.380
effect_direction: Lower EMQ scores indicate better subjective memory; rehabilitation and relaxation-control means were nearly identical.

Report_ID: Everyday Memory Questionnaire – patient version (EMQ-p) score at 6 months
Title: Group cognitive rehabilitation to reduce the psychological impact of multiple sclerosis on quality of life: the CRAMMS RCT
Author: Lincoln et al.
Comment: The paper explicitly reports the adjusted difference in means and 95% CI but the supplied results text does not provide EMQ-p outcome-specific analysed group Ns, follow-up means, or SDs, so these fields are null and no standardized effect was computed. SE_diff was derived from the reported 95% CI as (−1.9 − [−8.7])/3.92 = 1.735. The test statistic was then derived as M_diff/SE_diff = −3.055. The negative coefficient favors cognitive rehabilitation because higher EMQ-p scores indicate more frequent memory problems; synthesis direction should therefore be reversed when computing a positive-benefit standardized effect.; regression: no convertible statistic — need t-value for coefficient, b+SE(b), standardised β, r, η², or means+SDs
Design Type: Multicentre parallel-group pragmatic randomised controlled trial with multilevel adjusted analysis
domain: Cognitive rehabilitation for attention and memory problems in multiple sclerosis
Study Environment: Five NHS neurology-service sites in England; intervention sessions at NHS sites or community venues
Topic of Content: Restitution and compensatory strategies for attention and memory problems in daily life
interaction_type: Group intervention with four to six participants
Participant type: Adults aged 18–69 years with multiple sclerosis and self-reported and objectively identified cognitive problems
Recruitment source: NHS hospitals and participant identification centres, MS charities, public-facing study information, and the UK MS Register
Outcome measurement: EMQ-p: 28 items assessing frequency of everyday attention and memory failures over the previous month; total scores range from 0 to 112, with higher scores indicating more frequent memory problems
Outcome variable: Everyday Memory Questionnaire – patient version (EMQ-p) score at 6 months
effect_direction: The adjusted difference of -5.3 indicates fewer self-reported memory problems with cognitive rehabilitation and therefore favors rehabilitation.

Title: Efficacy of group cognitive rehabilitation therapy in multiple sclerosis
Author: Mani et al.
Comment: Hedges g (1.039), M_diff (6.87), and SE_diff (2.349) were calculated from the explicitly reported 3-month follow-up means, SDs, and final analyzed sample sizes. M_diff is intervention minus control (51.28 - 44.41), so positive values favor rehabilitation. Hedges g used the pooled post-score SD and small-sample correction. The reported p=.04 is labeled as the p-value for comparison between the two groups in the repeated-measures table and is not explicitly identified as a standalone 3-month follow-up contrast. No F statistic, degrees of freedom, adjusted estimate, confidence interval, or named effect measure was reported.
Design Type: Randomized controlled trial with repeated measures and blinded outcome assessment
domain: Multiple sclerosis cognitive rehabilitation; subjective memory
Study Environment: University-affiliated neurology and psychiatry clinics; group rehabilitation sessions
Topic of Content: Comprehensive compensatory cognitive rehabilitation focused on memory, attention, and executive function; sessions four to seven were dedicated to memory rehabilitation
interaction_type: Group cognitive rehabilitation versus matched non-therapeutic psychoeducation/sham group sessions
Participant type: Women aged 20-45 years with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis and cognitive impairment
Recruitment source: Emam Reza Neurology Clinic and a university-affiliated psychiatry clinic in Shiraz, Iran
Outcome measurement: Memory Functioning Questionnaire general rating subscale at 3-month follow-up
effect_direction: Higher MFQ general-rating scores indicate better perceived memory; the higher intervention mean favors cognitive rehabilitation.

Report_ID: Subjective everyday memory difficulties at four months
Title: Group memory rehabilitation for people with multiple sclerosis: a feasibility randomized controlled trial
Author: Carr et al.
Comment: The paper reports a Mann–Whitney U-test P value but not the U statistic. Hedges g was computed from the explicitly reported four-month means, SDs, and analysed group sizes: the sign was oriented so positive values indicate fewer subjective memory problems with rehabilitation because higher EMQ scores indicate worse memory. M_diff was computed as group_2 mean − group_1 mean (25.8 − 21.7 = 4.1), and SE_diff was computed as sqrt(13.1^2/17 + 19.9^2/21) = 5.381. Four months refers to time after randomization; because treatment lasted 10 weeks, this is approximately 1.5 months after treatment completion.
Content length: Ten 1.5-hour sessions over 10 weeks, with homework
Topic of Content: Attention training, internal memory strategies, external memory aids, and coping with everyday memory difficulties
interaction_type: Group rehabilitation delivered by an assistant psychologist
Participant type: People with multiple sclerosis who reported memory difficulties
Recruitment source: Register of patients attending Central Surrey Health multiple sclerosis clinics
Outcome measurement: Everyday Memory Questionnaire (EMQ-28), patient version; higher scores indicate more frequent memory problems
Outcome variable: Subjective everyday memory difficulties at four months
effect_direction: Lower EMQ scores indicate fewer memory problems; the lower rehabilitation mean favors rehabilitation.

Numerical baseline-to-long-term group change means and SDs are not stated in the supplied Results text and were not inferred from Figure 4, so a standardized mean difference/Hedges g cannot be calculated from the report text.; n_treatment(14) and n_control(14) inferred from t-test df=26

Report_ID: Subjective everyday memory functioning (Everyday Memory Questionnaire)
Title: Evaluation of Rehabilitation of Memory in Neurological Disabilities (ReMiND): a randomized controlled trial
Author: Roshan das Nair and Nadina B Lincoln
Comment: The paper reports only mixed-aetiology results, not a multiple-sclerosis-specific treatment effect. At baseline, the multiple-sclerosis counts were 12/24 in compensation, 17/24 in restitution, and 10/24 in self-help, but no diagnosis-stratified five-month outcome data were reported. Therefore this estimate cannot identify the effect specifically in people with multiple sclerosis. To avoid double-counting the shared control, the two eligible rehabilitation arms were combined from the explicitly reported five-month n, means, and SDs: combined n=44, mean=39.975, SD=22.121. Hedges g=0.118 was calculated from that combined arm and self-help, with direction reversed because lower frequency of everyday-memory slips represents better functioning. The paper did not report this Hedges g. M_diff and SE_diff were left null because this originated as a three-arm trial and the extraction rules prohibit computing a simple two-group M_diff by averaging/combining conditions. The Table 3 P=0.964 is an omnibus area-under-the-curve comparison over three assessments and was not entered as the P value for the selected five-month post-score effect.; excluded by outcome classification: does not match the requested outcome/timepoint (meta_analysis_candidate=False)
Study Environment: Community recruitment in the Nottingham and Derby area
Content length: Two individual sessions and ten weekly group sessions
Topic of Content: Internal memory aids, errorless learning, external aids in compensation, and encoding/retrieval and attention practice in restitution
Participant type: Adults with reported and demonstrable memory problems following traumatic brain injury, stroke, or multiple sclerosis
Recruitment source: Clinicians, charities, clinics, and stroke clubs
Outcome measurement: Unitary self-administered Everyday Memory Questionnaire measuring slips in normal memory function and real-life memory situations
Outcome variable: Subjective everyday memory functioning (Everyday Memory Questionnaire)
additional_group_ns: Compensation n=21; Restitution n=23; Self-help n=23 at five months
effect_direction: Lower EMQ scores indicate fewer memory problems; the combined rehabilitation-arm mean is lower than the self-help mean and nominally favors rehabilitation.

Title: Evaluation of cognitive rehabilitation on the cognitive performance in multiple sclerosis: A randomized controlled trial
Author: Shahpouri et al.
Comment: The paper reports significance as 0.000; this was recorded verbatim and should be interpreted as below the software display threshold, not as an exact zero probability. The ANCOVA F test is baseline-adjusted, but the displayed group means and SDs are unadjusted posttest values from Table 2. No adjusted means, adjusted mean difference, standard error of the treatment contrast, confidence interval, or standardized effect size is reported. Timing is described inconsistently as within 3 months after study initiation versus over 3 months after the intervention; exact time since treatment completion is unclear. Lower PRMQ scores appear to reflect fewer memory problems, but the Results do not explicitly state the scale direction.
Design Type: Double-blinded randomized controlled clinical trial with pretest/posttest assessment and ANCOVA
Study Environment: Kashani MS Clinic affiliated to Isfahan University of Medical Sciences
Content length: Ten sessions; 2 hours per session; every 7–10 days
Topic of Content: Attention, concentration, visual and auditory memory, autobiographical memory, and mnemonic/compensatory strategies
Recruitment source: Patients referred to Kashani MS Clinic
Outcome measurement: Prospective and Retrospective Memory Questionnaire (16-item questionnaire)
effect_direction: Lower PRMQ scores appear to indicate fewer subjective memory failures; the lower rehabilitation mean therefore favors rehabilitation.

Table 2 does not report outcome-specific analyzed sample sizes. EMQ means and SDs are not reported, so a standardized mean difference/Hedges g cannot be calculated from this report. The assessment-group median was 18.5 (IQR 5–31), but that arm is not entered as an eligible treatment group for this synthesis.; unsupported or insufficient statistic type
